slides: Open by telling students that four-dimensional geometry becomes usable when we choose representations with explicit losses. The tesseract shadow preserves incidence but distorts length, sections reveal only one level at a time, and tables protect the invisible dimensions with counts and invariants.

Use this route slide to keep the lecture from becoming a gallery of strange objects. The chapter moves from projected figures to sliced figures, then to regular four-polytope bookkeeping, honeycomb symbol tests, the D4 packing shell, statistical cells, and a small parameter lab.

The tesseract slide should be taught as a controlled shadow rather than a picture of four-space. Students can count sixteen vertices and thirty-two edges, compare near and far cubic facets, and notice that the eight connector edges are the reliable combinatorial bridge.

Slicing the sixteen-cell gives a concrete way to see a four-dimensional object by ordinary three-dimensional cross sections. Fixing w equals t leaves an octahedron whose scale is one minus absolute t, so the shape stays combinatorial while volume changes cubically.

The regular four-polytope table is the stabilizing reference point for the chapter. Vertices, edges, faces, and cells are all counted separately, and the boundary Euler check V minus E plus F minus C equals zero prevents students from treating faces and cells interchangeably.

Honeycomb symbols encode local regularity with the triple p, q, r. The local polyhedron checks make sure the facet and vertex figure are finite, while the margin separates spherical finite cases, the Euclidean boundary, and hyperbolic candidates in the sampled table.

The D4 packing slide connects four-dimensional geometry to a measurement problem: how many equal spheres can touch one central sphere. The root shell has twenty-four equal-distance neighbors, minimum center distance square root two, and packing density about zero point six one seven.

The statistical honeycomb slide deliberately contrasts a perfect symbol with sampled cell data. Instead of one regular rule, the Voronoi proxy gives a distribution of side counts and areas, so students should inspect the spread rather than search for a single ideal cell.

The section-volume lab is the hands-on parameter experiment for the lecture. Moving the slicing plane changes only the fourth-coordinate level, and the normalized volume curve checks the cubic law across thirty-nine samples while preserving the octahedral section combinatorics.

Close by summarizing the discipline of representation. Projection, section, f-vector, symbol, packing shell, and statistical sample each forget something different, so the mathematical work is to pair every visual with the invariant it is still allowed to claim.
